verses.text: “Why aren’t times laid up by the Almighty? Why don’t those who know him see his days?
There are people who remove the landmarks. They violently take away flocks, and feed them.
They drive away the donkey of the fatherless, and they take the widow’s ox for a pledge.
They turn the needy out of the way. The poor of the earth all hide themselves.
Behold, as wild donkeys in the desert, they go out to their work, seeking diligently for food. The wilderness yields them bread for their children.
They cut their food in the field. They glean the vineyard of the wicked.
They lie all night naked without clothing, and have no covering in the cold.
They are wet with the showers of the mountains, and embrace the rock for lack of a shelter.
There are those who pluck the fatherless from the breast, and take a pledge of the poor,
So that they go around naked without clothing. Being hungry, they carry the sheaves.
They make oil within the walls of these men. They tread wine presses, and suffer thirst.
From out of the populous city, men groan. The soul of the wounded cries out, yet God doesn’t regard the folly.
“These are of those who rebel against the light. They don’t know its ways, nor stay in its paths.
The murderer rises with the light. He kills the poor and needy. In the night he is like a thief.
The eye also of the adulterer waits for the twilight, saying, ‘No eye shall see me.’ He disguises his face.
In the dark they dig through houses. They shut themselves up in the daytime. They don’t know the light.
For the morning is to all of them like thick darkness, for they know the terrors of the thick darkness.
“They are foam on the surface of the waters. Their portion is cursed in the earth. They don’t turn into the way of the vineyards.
Drought and heat consume the snow waters, so does Sheol  those who have sinned.
The womb shall forget him. The worm shall feed sweetly on him. He shall be no more remembered. Unrighteousness shall be broken as a tree.
He devours the barren who don’t bear. He shows no kindness to the widow.
Yet God preserves the mighty by his power. He rises up who has no assurance of life.
God gives them security, and they rest in it. His eyes are on their ways.
They are exalted; yet a little while, and they are gone. Yes, they are brought low, they are taken out of the way as all others, and are cut off as the tops of the ears of grain.
If it isn’t so now, who will prove me a liar, and make my speech worth nothing?”

footnotes.content: Job asks the hardest question: if God is good and almighty, why does He not judge wickedness now? This is the ache at the heart of the book—a heart that trusts God yet cannot yet see His hand at work.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Theft of landmarks—the markers of rightful ownership—speaks to a world turned upside down by greed. Those who move boundaries steal not just land but a family's future and inheritance.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The widow and fatherless had no advocates in that world—no husband to shield them, no father to fight for them. The law of Moses made protecting them sacred work. That this verse describes their plunder shows the depth of the corruption Job witnesses.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Notice the pattern: the powerful push the needy out of paths and roads, and the poor retreat into hiding. Injustice makes victims invisible to the very society that should welcome them.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: These poor toil in the wilderness like wild donkeys—driven out from settled land, forced to scavenge their children's bread where no one else ventures. There is dignity in their work, but it speaks of desperation.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Gleaning leftovers from an evil man's vineyard—this is what the dispossessed must do. Even the charity of gleaning law becomes survival scraps when true justice has vanished from the land.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: To lie naked in the cold is to know want in its rawest form. Job catalogs this suffering not to despair but to show the world he sees—and to ask why God seems silent as it happens.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Mountain rains soak them; stone embraces them as shelter. This is not poetry to Job—it is the geography of homelessness, the stone-cold indifference of nature to human suffering.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: To pluck a nursing child from its mother's arms is to show cruelty at its absolute core—not taking bread but taking life's very thread. The wickedness here is unspeakable.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Stripped of clothing, hollow with hunger, yet forced to carry sheaves of grain—there is bitter irony in their labor. They harvest wealth they will never taste while their children go naked.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The poor press oil and wine—they create abundance for others. But they suffer thirst, knowing exactly what they produce and exactly who gets to drink it. This is the cruelty of injustice.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: From cities, groans rise. The wounded cry out. And the text says God does not charge the wrongdoers with folly—this may be Job's deepest complaint. Where is judgment? Where is accountability?
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: To rebel against light is to choose darkness knowingly. These are not victims of circumstance but rebels who have turned away from truth and chosen their own crooked paths.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Murder at dawn, theft at night—the wicked make time itself their accomplice. They divide their wickedness by daylight and darkness, showing calculation, not impulse.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The adulterer watches for twilight, masks his face—all his craft goes into hiding his desire. He knows his sin and works to conceal it, showing that the wicked are not innocently lost but willfully deceptive.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: To dig through houses in darkness, to shut yourself away from daylight—the criminals Job describes are not desperate but driven into shadow by choice, hiding who they really are.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Morning arrives like thick darkness to them—they know terrors in broad daylight that others never dream of. Their conscience has become their prison; light brings no comfort, only dread.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Foam on water—here is their final state, spoken as a turning. After all Job's suffering witness, he begins to declare what becomes of the wicked: they are cursed, unstable, empty. Like sea foam, they vanish.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Drought and heat melt the snow; Sheol comes for the sinful the same way. No escape, no hiding place—what melts the mountains will come for those who rebel against light.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The womb forgets them; worms claim them; unrighteousness breaks like a dead tree. This is the fate Job declares—not a threat but a promise: the wicked are remembered by none, eaten by none, cut off as surely as rotted wood.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The cruel man devours the barren, shows no kindness to widows—this sums his evil. Where the law calls for protection of the vulnerable, his nature tends toward predation.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Yet God preserves the mighty—a turn that will puzzle readers. Even those who seem assured of nothing, God upholds. In the midst of injustice, the Lord's power still moves, still sustains, still sees.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Readers today hear an echo in this: God gives security not as a sign of approval but as part of His sovereign keeping. He lets them rest, yet His eyes remain upon their ways. We learn, as Job does, that God's watching is not absence—it is a judgment written in silence.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Exalted for a moment, then gone—like grain tops cut at harvest. This is the brevity of the wicked's triumph. They rise, but only to be gathered and cast out as all others are.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Job's final question: if this is not so, who can prove him a liar? He has spoken what he has seen, and the truth of his witness stands. His complaint is not despair but the cry of one who cannot help but speak.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
